subject: money
topic: Lottery tickets are bought most by those with least
angle: While lottery spending is strongly linked to poverty and regressive taxes, the regressivity of instant games varies significantly by price point.
title: The Economics of Hope

hooks.text: Why do the poorest people play the most?
You think it is a game of luck. The data shows it is a regressive tax.
You are paying a price you cannot afford.
A small ticket held in a trembling hand.
Lottery spending is linked to poverty.

reveal.headline: Low income fuels the highest lottery participation.
reveal.body: People with the least money play the most. They pay a regressive tax on games that cost them more relative to their income.

explain.headline: Price points change the tax burden.
explain.body: Lower-priced games are more regressive. Higher-priced games show less variance in sales based on household income levels.

matters.headline: Income perception shapes your choices.
matters.body: That may be why you buy a ticket. When you perceive your income as low relative to an implicit standard, you are more likely to purchase.

example.headline: The corner store at dusk.
example.body: You stand under a flickering light. You hold a few coins. You pick up a small ticket to see if your life changes tonight.

question.headline: What are you looking for in that ticket?

stat.label: tax burden on instant lottery games

claims.text: Higher-priced instant games are less regressive than lower-priced games.
claims.quote: the empirical results show that higher-priced instant games are less regressive than lower-priced games.

claims.text: Counties having a higher-percentage of low-income households have higher sales of lower-priced instant games, but differences in the distribution of household income have no significant impact on higher-priced instant sales.
claims.quote: counties having a higher-percentage of low-income households have higher sales of lower-priced instant games, but differences in the distribution of household income have no significant impact on higher-priced instant sales.

claims.text: Priming low-income participants to perceive their own income as low relative to an implicit standard causes them to be more likely to purchase lottery tickets.
claims.quote: participants were more likely to purchase lottery tickets when they were primed to perceive that their own income was low relative to an implicit standard.

claims.text: The taxes on all lottery games are regressive, with instant games having the greatest regressivity.
claims.quote: The authors find that the taxes on all lottery games are regressive, with instant games having the greatest regressivity

claims.text: State lotteries are extremely popular among the poor, who play the most but can least afford to play.
claims.quote: state lotteries are extremely popular, especially among the poor, who play the most but can least afford to play.

claims.text: Lottery expenditures are linked to income, location of the household, gender, age, education, social class and whether the household has positive betting expenditures.
claims.quote: Lottery expenditures are affected by income, location of the household, gender, age, education, social class and whether the household has positive betting expenditures.

verdict: The evidence consistently shows that lower-income individuals participate more in lotteries and face a regressive tax burden, though higher-priced games may be less regressive.
caveat: One study notes that the relationship between lottery sales and poverty is an association and does not prove causation.
caption:
Lottery spending is tied to income and social class.

Research shows that lower-income individuals participate more and face a regressive tax burden, though higher-priced games may be less regressive. One study notes that the relationship between lottery sales and poverty is an association and does not prove causation.
